**NORTH BATTLEFORD, Saskatchewan (CNN)** — A two-decade dream dissolved into the clear Canadian sky on Tuesday when a French adventurer’s attempt to set a world record for the highest space jump ended in heartbreaking failure—before he even left the ground. 

Michel Fournier, a 64-year-old retired French army officer, watched helplessly from inside a tracking trailer as his massive, multi-million-dollar helium balloon detached prematurely, inflated, and floated away into the atmosphere empty.

Fournier had been preparing to launch "Le Grand Saut" (The Big Jump), an ambitious attempt to ascend to an altitude of 130,000 feet (nearly 40 kilometers) in a pressurized capsule suspended beneath a massive, tissue-thin polyethylene balloon. 

Once at the edge of space, he planned to step out of the capsule and plunge toward Earth in a specialized suit, aiming to become the first human to break the sound barrier in freefall without an aircraft. 

Instead, a technical malfunction during the final stages of pre-launch preparation brought a sudden and dramatic end to the mission on the tarmac of the North Battleford airport in Saskatchewan, Canada. 

According to project officials, Fournier was already suited up in his chest-high, pressurized space suit and preparing to step into the capsule when the balloon unexpectedly separated from the payload and rapidly ascended into the sky.

"The balloon just took off without the capsule," said a visibly shaken member of Fournier’s support team. "We don’t know why the automatic detachment system triggered. It is a absolute disaster."

The rogue balloon drifted toward the east, leaving Fournier stranded on the ground, surrounded by months of preparation and tens of thousands of onlookers tuning in globally via internet livestreams. 

The abort marks a devastating setback for Fournier, who has spent more than 20 years and roughly $20 million of his own money trying to pull off the feat. To finance the project, Fournier sold his home and liquid assets, driven by a singular obsession to break the high-altitude jump record set in 1960 by U.S. Air Force Officer Joe Kittinger, who jumped from 102,800 feet.

This is not the first time bad luck has plagued the French aviator. In 2002 and 2003, Fournier made similar attempts in France and Canada, both of which were scuttled when his balloons tore during the delicate inflation process. 

Beyond the personal disappointment, Tuesday’s failure carries a heavy financial toll. The custom-built balloon alone cost an estimated $200,000 and cannot be reused. With a limited weather window for high-altitude attempts in Saskatchewan and dwindling funds, it remains unclear whether Fournier will ever get another chance to realize his dream.

Prior to the launch attempt, Fournier had framed the jump not just as an adrenaline-fueled stunt, but as a scientific mission intended to test survival equipment for future astronauts and space tourists facing high-altitude emergencies.

As the uncrewed balloon vanished into the upper atmosphere, team members escorted a silent Fournier away from the launch pad. The team has launched an investigation to determine why the release mechanism triggered prematurely.

**NORTH BATTLEFORD, Saskatchewan (CNN) —** A harrowing turn of events shattered months of preparation and a multi-million-dollar dream on Tuesday morning, as an attempt to execute the highest skydiving jump in human history was abruptly aborted following a catastrophic balloon failure on the remote plains of western Canada.

Unusually sharp atmospheric conditions ripped through the launch site near North Battleford, Saskatchewan, tearing the 400-foot polyethylene envelope like tissue paper and releasing hundreds of thousands of cubic feet of helium into the freezing morning air. 

Vance, 42, was quickly extracted from the capsule by ground crew members. He was uninjured, but visible emotional strain washed over his face as he surveyed the shredded, white remains of the balloon drifting across the airfield. 

**[WATCH: The heart-stopping moment a 400-foot space balloon tears apart on the Canadian launchpad]**

### 'A heartbreak you can't prepare for'

"You train for years, you simulate every nightmare scenario in the air, but you never expect the sky to fight back before you even leave the ground," Vance told CNN’s Anderson Cooper shortly after the incident. 

"I was in the suit, pre-breathing pure oxygen, focused on the jump. Then I heard a sound like a freight train passing right over us—a massive, snapping crack. The next thing I knew, the ground crew was screaming 'Abort, abort, abort!' It’s a heartbreak you simply can't prepare for."

Vance’s mission, dubbed *Project Zenith*, was aimed at breaking the current world record for the highest freefall jump, set in 2014 by Alan Eustace at 135,890 feet. 

**[RELATED: Felix Baumgartner to Alan Eustace: A history of daring jumps from the edge of space]**

### A 'one-in-a-million' freak accident

While high-altitude balloons are notoriously fragile, meteorologists and aerospace experts on site described the event as a "freak atmospheric anomaly."

The balloon's envelope—made of high-density polyethylene that is thinner than a typical plastic sandwich bag—is designed to withstand extreme pressure in the stratosphere, but it is extraordinarily vulnerable during the initial inflation phase on the ground.

Dr. Aris Thorne, a senior aerodynamicist at the International Stratospheric Institute and technical consultant for the mission, explained that a sudden, hyper-localized microburst caught the balloon at a critical moment.

"What we witnessed was a catastrophic confluence of three factors," Dr. Thorne told CNN. "First, an undetected low-level wind shear created a lateral pull on the top section of the balloon while the base was secured. Second, the extreme cold snap in Saskatchewan this morning rendered the plastic slightly more brittle than baseline. Finally, we believe a static discharge ignited a shockwave through the shifting plastic, causing a tear along the primary seam."

Dr. Thorne emphasized that pre-launch sensor sweeps had shown pristine ground conditions just ten minutes prior. "It was a one-in-a-million atmospheric roll of the dice. A complete freak accident."

**[WATCH: 'Thinner than a sandwich bag': Experts break down the science behind stratospheric balloon failures]**

### $15 million up in smoke

The failed attempt carries a staggering price tag. The total cost of *Project Zenith* stands at an estimated $15 million, backed largely by a consortium of tech venture capitalists and extreme sports sponsors.

According to team logistics directors, the balloon alone cost upwards of $700,000 and cannot be reused. Additionally, the mission consumed roughly 800,000 cubic feet of industrial-grade helium—a resource currently plagued by a global shortage, costing the team nearly $1.2 million for this single attempt.

"The financial gut-punch is immense," said Sarah Lin, the project’s lead coordinator. "The capsule and the life-support systems are fine, but the helium loss and the destruction of the envelope mean we are looking at millions of dollars literally vanishing into the breeze. Insurance covers part of it, but getting another custom balloon fabricated and securing that much helium again will take at least six to eight months."

### 'We will try again'

For Vance, the financial hit and the psychological blow are heavy, but he insists his dream of touching the stars and stepping into the void isn't dead.

"We built a capsule that works. We built a suit that keeps me alive in a vacuum. Nature caught us off guard today, plain and simple," Vance said, staring out at the Canadian prairie as recovery crews packed away the debris. 

"We take a breather, we analyze the telemetry, and we raise the funds. I didn’t come all the way to Canada just to watch a balloon pop. We *will* get to 135,000 feet."

**[WATCH: 'We live to fly another day' — Full interview with skydiver Alex Vance after aborted launch]**

# Heartbreak in Canada: French Adventurer’s Balloon Escapes Before Record ‘Big Jump’

**NORTH BATTLEFORD, Saskatchewan** — French daredevil Michel Fournier’s multi-million-dollar quest to jump from the edge of space ended in devastating failure early Tuesday morning, not because of a mechanical malfunction in mid-air, but because his giant helium balloon unexpectedly detached and drifted into the sky without him.

Fournier, 64, a retired French army parachutist, was already suited up in his pressurized astronaut-style gear and sitting inside his launch capsule when the massive, ultra-thin plastic balloon suddenly detached during the final stages of inflation. 

Ground crew members and onlookers watched in stunned silence as the $200,000 balloon—capable of expanding to the size of a football field—silently soared into the cloudless blue Canadian sky, eventually vanishing toward the east empty-handed.

"It's over for today," a visibly shaken team spokesperson told reporters gathered at the North Battleford airport. "The balloon just took off without the capsule."

### A Lifetime Dream Deflated

The aborted mission, dubbed *Le Grand Saut* (The Big Jump), was meant to be the culmination of nearly two decades of preparation and millions of dollars in private sponsorship. 

Fournier had intended to ride the balloon into the stratosphere to an unprecedented altitude of 40,000 meters (130,000 feet)—roughly three times the cruising altitude of a commercial airliner. Once there, he planned to step out of his pressurized capsule and plummet back to Earth in a freefall lasting nearly six minutes, becoming the first human to break the speed of sound without an aircraft.

Had he succeeded, Fournier would have shattered four world records, including the highest altitude jump, the longest freefall, and the highest manned balloon flight—a record held since 1960 by U.S. Air Force Captain Joe Kittinger (102,800 feet).

Instead, the retired soldier sat trapped inside his pressurized capsule on the tarmac, forced to watch his chance at history float away. 

### Cruel Luck in the Canadian Plains

Engineers and safety officials on site immediately launched an investigation into why the reserve mechanism triggered the detachment of the balloon from the capsule while still on the ground. Weather conditions at dawn had been described as near-perfect, with light winds and high visibility.

This was not Fournier's first encounter with bad luck in his pursuit of the stratosphere:
* **In 2002**, a previous balloon attempt in France ended when strong winds shredded the delicate plastic envelope during inflation.
* **In 2003**, another attempt was called off after the balloon tore just as it was being filled with helium.

Tuesday’s failure was particularly crushing because Fournier had spent years securing Canadian permits, passing rigorous physical exams, and waiting out unpredictable weather on the Saskatchewan plains. 

### An Uncertain Future

The financial impact of Tuesday's mishap is severe. The custom-built, ultra-light stratospheric balloons used for such attempts are one-time-use items and take months to manufacture. 

When asked if Fournier would attempt the jump again, team members were hesitant to give a definitive answer, citing the immediate need to secure another balloon and additional funding. 

Despite the immense disappointment, supporters praised Fournier’s courage. 

"Michel is a man of incredible courage and determination," said one of the project's lead engineers. "To get this close, to be sitting in the suit ready to go, and to have a technical fluke ruin it... it is a nightmare. But if anyone has the grit to bounce back, it is him."

As the runaway balloon drifted somewhere over eastern Canada—destined to eventually pop and fall to the ground—a exhausted Fournier was assisted out of his heavy suit, his dream of touching the stars delayed once again.

*** 

*Note: Michel Fournier spent over $20 million of his own money and sponsor funds over his lifetime trying to achieve "Le Grand Saut." He was never able to successfully launch, and the record for the highest space jump was later claimed by Felix Baumgartner in 2012 (38,969m) and subsequently broken by Alan Eustace in 2014 (41,419m).*
